section_1.title: Introduction: The Putnam Mindset (30 seconds)
section_1.content: Briefly introduce the competition's philosophy: it’s not about rote calculation, but about finding elegant, hidden structural patterns. Define the core objective: 'Reduction to Simplicity'.
section_1.example: An animated clock gear mechanism where many teeth turn; focus on the single point of rotation, not the complexity of every gear.

section_2.title: Prerequisite: The Concept of Invariance (60 seconds)
section_2.content: Define an 'Invariant'—a property of a system that remains unchanged under specific operations. Visual representation: A dynamic graph showing an object deforming while its area or centroid stays fixed.
section_2.example: A group of chameleons on an island. If two change color, the parity of the count of each color remains invariant, preventing them from all becoming the same color.

section_3.title: Core Strategy: Exploiting Symmetry (90 seconds)
section_3.content: How to identify symmetry in polynomials and functional equations. Visual: Split-screen showing an asymmetric equation transformed into a mirror-image system via a variable substitution.
section_3.example: Solving a complex functional equation using the 'f(x) + f(1-x) = 1' symmetry rule, visualized as a balance beam pivoting at 0.5.

section_4.title: Application: The Pigeonhole Principle & Extremal Methods (90 seconds)
section_4.content: Applying the Pigeonhole Principle to bound outcomes. Introduce 'Extremal' thinking: analyzing the 'largest' or 'smallest' element to force a contradiction in the proof.
section_4.example: A robotic vacuum cleaner navigating a room with fixed obstacles; use the 'most distant point' from the wall to prove the robot must revisit a tile.

section_5.title: Closing: Verification & Final Polish (30 seconds)
section_5.content: Summary of the 'Check-Back' technique: verify boundary conditions and trivial cases to ensure the elegant solution is mathematically rigorous.
section_5.example: A character placing a 'Golden Key' into a lock; the key represents the final proof step that fits perfectly into the problem statement.
